newsitem.title: PERU: Peru crisis far from a solution despite prayers.
newsitem.headline: Peru crisis far from a solution despite prayers.

text.p: The 19-day standoff between the Peruvian government and Marxist guerrillas holding 74 VIP hostages looked farther than ever from a solution on Sunday despite fervent prayers at home and abroad for a bloodless end.
Pope John Paul II, in an apparent appeal to the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels, urged kidnappers and hostage-takers to free their captives as a "gesture of humanity."
"The mercy of Christ, born of human weakness, urges hostage-takers to fulfil this gesture of humanity -- free these people," the pope told pilgrims in St Peter's Square at his regular Sunday address.
From tiny Andean churches to large city congregations, Peruvians prayed and held vigils for the captives.
"I have faith that everything is going to change," chanted rosary-bearing nuns outside the besieged Japanese residence, while inside Catholic bishop Juan Luis Cipriani gave mass to the captive men.
But the prayers appeared to fall on deaf ears as both sides in the conflict remained locked in their longest stalemate yet -- four days with no new releases or talks.

Other than Cipriani's entry, the only activity at the mined and booby-trapped residence was the usual shuttling to and fro of Red Cross officials with medicines, food and other supplies such as books, cleaning materials and cigarettes.

The guerrillas have not released any more hostages since New Year's Day, and Fujimori has kept his negotiator, Domingo Palermo, away from the residence after a first face-to-face meeting eight days ago.
Neither side relaxed its uncompromising position, with the MRTA maintaining a demand for the release of some 400 jailed comrades and Fujimori flatly refusing.

"Both the MRTA and the government through President Fujimori have shown irreconcilable positions," said opposition legislator Maximo San Roman Caceres, a former Peruvian vice president under Fujimori.
"The process of dialogue ... has become bogged down, and there is no immediate solution," he said. "It is putting at serious risk the life of many human beings."
Reflecting the growing desperation in Peru for a solution from any quarter, San Roman proposed that the pope mediate an end to the crisis.

Another legislator proposed veteran crisis-broker and former U.S. President Jimmy Carter be called in, while the rebels said they would accept Cuban President Fidel Castro or Russian leader Boris Yeltsin.
Bolivian Foreign Minister Antonio Aranibar arrived in Lima on Sunday to try to help bring about a solution. Bolivian ambassador Jorge Gumucio is among the captives.

At a news conference, Aranibar backed Fujimori's tough position and ruled out releasing four MRTA prisoners in Bolivia. But he appealed to the rebels to care for Gumucio who "suffers from high blood pressure, is diabetic, requiring special care, and also has in his medical history a heart attack."

Gumucio and Japanese envoy Morihisa Aoki are the only two ambassadors left in the residence. Their fellow hostages include Fujimori's brother, top Peruvian government officials and about two dozen Japanese diplomats and businessmen.
The standoff began on Dec. 17 when about 20 well-armed MRTA rebels burst in to a cocktail party honouring Japanese Emperor Akihito's birthday that was attended by 500 people.
In defiant banners unfurled on the residence roof over the weekend, the rebels insisted they were open to dialogue, but lambasted Fujimori for "arrogance."
"Nobody in here is giving up" read one of the messages. "Mr Fujimori, with arrogant declarations and without dialogue, there will never be a solution," said another.
On Thursday Fujimori virulently rejected the rebels' claim to be fighting for Peru's poor and condemned them as "terrorists" bent on "feverish, destructive" violence.

A Japanese newspaper reported on Sunday that the MRTA rebels were demanding up to $30 million in ransom from Japanese firms whose executives they hold. But Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto said he was not aware of any ransom demands and that the government had not been approached.

Red Cross spokesman Ronald Bigler told Reuters the organisation maintained its offer of being an intermediary for information in the crisis. But he said the Red Cross could only be of limited help in reaching agreement over the main sticking points in the crisis.
"Eventually it must come to face-to-face talks," he said.
